Vestibular suppressants (prochlorperazine, antihistamines) — not recommended for BPPV specifically as they do not treat the underlying cause. Surgical canal plugging — reserved for refractory cases. Most cases resolve spontaneously within weeks to months.

title: Nasal fracture – Clinical features and management
content: Nasal fracture is the most common facial fracture. Mechanism: direct trauma. Features: nasal pain and tenderness, epistaxis, nasal deformity (deviation, depression), periorbital bruising, nasal obstruction. Examination: assess for nasal septal haematoma (boggy bilateral swelling of nasal septum — requires urgent drainage). Management: analgesia; ice pack; nasal fracture reduction — ideally performed at 5–10 days (after swelling subsides but before bony union). Refer to ENT if: septal haematoma, significant deformity, suspected CSF rhinorrhoea.

title: Deviated nasal septum – Clinical features and management
content: Deviated nasal septum (DNS): deviation of the nasal septum from the midline. May be congenital or acquired (trauma). Features: unilateral or bilateral nasal obstruction; recurrent sinusitis; snoring; epistaxis (from turbulent airflow). Management: medical (intranasal corticosteroids, decongestants); surgical — septoplasty (surgical straightening of nasal septum); may be combined with turbinate reduction (septorhinoplasty if cosmetic correction also required).

title: Snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea – Pathophysiology and assessment
content: Snoring results from vibration of soft tissues of the upper airway during sleep. Obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is characterised by repeated episodes of partial or complete upper airway obstruction during sleep causing apnoeas (≥10 seconds cessation of airflow) or hypopnoeas (≥50% reduction in airflow). Risk factors: obesity (most important), male sex, age, alcohol, sedatives, smoking, enlarged tonsils/adenoids, retrognathia, macroglossia. Assessment: Epworth Sleepiness Scale; polysomnography (gold standard) or overnight oximetry (screening). AHI (apnoea-hypopnoea index): mild 5–14, moderate 15–29, severe ≥30 events/hour.

title: Snoring and obstructive sleep apnoea – Clinical features and management
content: OSA clinical features: loud snoring (reported by partner), witnessed apnoeas, excessive daytime sleepiness (Epworth score >10), morning headaches, poor concentration, nocturia, reduced libido, irritability. Complications: hypertension, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, road traffic accidents. Management: lifestyle modification (weight loss, alcohol avoidance, positional therapy); CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure — gold standard for moderate-severe OSA); mandibular advancement device (mild-moderate); surgical options (uvulopalatopharyngoplasty, tonsillectomy if enlarged tonsils, nasal surgery). DVLA notification required if excessive daytime sleepiness.

title: Facial palsy (Bell's palsy) – Definition and aetiology
content: Bell's palsy is an acute, idiopathic, unilateral lower motor neurone facial nerve (CN VII) palsy. Incidence: 20–30 per 100,000 per year. Peak incidence: 15–45 years. Aetiology: idiopathic (most common); associated with HSV-1 reactivation (most evidence); other causes of facial palsy: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (VZV reactivation — vesicular rash in ear), Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, parotid tumour, cholesteatoma, acoustic neuroma, stroke (UMN — forehead sparing), Guillain-Barré syndrome.

title: Facial palsy (Bell's palsy) – Clinical features
content: Bell's palsy features: unilateral LMN facial weakness (all branches affected — forehead involved, distinguishing from UMN/stroke); drooping of mouth; inability to close eye (lagophthalmos — risk of corneal exposure); loss of forehead wrinkling; altered taste (anterior 2/3 tongue — chorda tympani); hyperacusis (stapedius branch); reduced lacrimation; post-auricular pain (often precedes palsy). House-Brackmann grading scale used to assess severity (I = normal, VI = complete paralysis).

title: Facial palsy (Bell's palsy) – Management and prognosis
content: Management of Bell's palsy: oral prednisolone (started within 72 hours of onset — improves recovery rate; NICE recommends 50 mg/day for 10 days); antivirals (aciclovir or valaciclovir — added to steroids if severe palsy, though evidence less strong); eye care (artificial tears, lubricating eye ointment at night, eye patch or tape if unable to close eye — prevents corneal exposure). Prognosis: 85% recover completely within 3 weeks to 3 months; 15% have incomplete recovery; poor prognostic factors: complete paralysis, age >60, hypertension, diabetes, severe pain.

title: Croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) – Definition and clinical features
content: Croup is a viral infection of the upper respiratory tract causing subglottic oedema and airway obstruction. Most common cause: parainfluenza virus. Predominantly affects children aged 6 months–3 years. Features: prodromal URTI; characteristic barking cough ('seal-like'); inspiratory stridor; hoarse voice; low-grade fever; symptoms typically worse at night. Westley croup score used to assess severity. Croup score: mild (0–2), moderate (3–7), severe (≥8).

title: Croup – Management
content: Management of croup: mild — reassurance, oral dexamethasone (0.15 mg/kg single dose); moderate — oral/IM dexamethasone (0.15–0.6 mg/kg), nebulised adrenaline (1:1000, 0.5 mL/kg up to 5 mL) for immediate relief; severe — as above plus hospital admission, oxygen, consider intubation. Nebulised budesonide alternative to dexamethasone. Avoid distressing child (crying worsens obstruction). Humidified air — no evidence of benefit.

title: Epiglottitis – Definition, aetiology and clinical features
content: Epiglottitis is a life-threatening infection causing acute inflammation and oedema of the epiglottis and supraglottic structures. Most common causative organism: Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) — now rare due to vaccination; Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae in adults. Peak incidence: 2–7 years (children); adults increasingly affected. Features: rapid onset (hours); high fever; severe sore throat; dysphagia; drooling (inability to swallow saliva); muffled 'hot potato' voice; stridor (late sign); tripod position (leaning forward, neck extended); toxic appearance. Do NOT examine throat — may precipitate complete obstruction.

title: Epiglottitis – Investigations and management
content: Epiglottitis investigations: lateral neck X-ray (thumb sign — enlarged epiglottis; only if diagnosis uncertain and patient stable); direct laryngoscopy under GA (gold standard — shows cherry-red swollen epiglottis). Management: EMERGENCY — call anaesthetist and ENT surgeon immediately; secure airway (intubation or tracheostomy); IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone or co-amoxiclav); IV dexamethasone (reduce oedema); oxygen; IV fluids. Admit to ICU. Do NOT attempt throat examination, IV access, or distress patient before airway secured.

title: Infectious mononucleosis – Aetiology and epidemiology
content: Infectious mononucleosis (glandular fever) is caused by Epstein-Barr virus (EBV, human herpesvirus 4). Incidence: 45 per 100,000 person-years. Peak incidence: 15–24 years. Sex ratio 1:1. Transmission: saliva ('kissing disease'). EBV infects B lymphocytes via CD21 receptor → polyclonal B cell activation → atypical lymphocytes (Downey cells) → heterophile antibody production.

title: Infectious mononucleosis – Clinical features
content: Infectious mononucleosis features: prodrome (1–2 weeks — fatigue, malaise, anorexia); fever; sore throat (exudative tonsillitis — may be severe); lymphadenopathy (posterior cervical most characteristic; also anterior cervical, axillary, inguinal); splenomegaly (50% — risk of splenic rupture); hepatomegaly (10–15%); rash (maculopapular — 10–15%; almost universal if given amoxicillin/ampicillin); palatal petechiae; periorbital oedema. Complications: splenic rupture (0.1–0.5%), airway obstruction from tonsillar hypertrophy, haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopaenia, hepatitis, meningitis, encephalitis, Guillain-Barré.

title: Infectious mononucleosis – Investigations and management
content: Investigations for infectious mononucleosis: monospot test (Paul-Bunnell test — detects heterophile antibodies; sensitivity 85%, specificity 100%; may be negative in first week); FBC (lymphocytosis with >10% atypical lymphocytes); LFTs (elevated in 80%); EBV-specific antibodies (VCA IgM — confirms acute infection; EBNA IgG — past infection). Management: supportive (rest, analgesia, adequate hydration); avoid contact sports for 4 weeks (splenic rupture risk); avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin (causes rash); corticosteroids if severe tonsillar hypertrophy causing airway compromise. Return to sport: 4 weeks minimum, longer if splenomegaly persists.

title: Ear wax (cerumen impaction) – Clinical features and management
content: Ear wax (cerumen) impaction: common cause of conductive hearing loss. Features: hearing loss, tinnitus, otalgia, sensation of fullness, dizziness. Otoscopy: brown/yellow waxy material occluding canal. Management: softening agents (olive oil, sodium bicarbonate drops — 3–5 days before irrigation); ear irrigation (syringing — contraindicated if perforation, previous ear surgery, or recurrent otitis externa); manual removal (microsuction — preferred in ENT; Jobson-Horne probe). Prevention: avoid cotton buds (push wax deeper); regular softening drops if prone to impaction.

title: Noise-induced hearing loss – Pathophysiology and management
content: Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL): caused by damage to cochlear hair cells from prolonged or acute loud noise exposure. Characteristic audiometric pattern: notch at 4 kHz (then 3 and 6 kHz). Temporary threshold shift (TTS): reversible hearing loss after acute noise exposure. Permanent threshold shift (PTS): irreversible loss after repeated exposure. Tinnitus often accompanies NIHL. Management: hearing protection (primary prevention); hearing aids; tinnitus management; occupational health referral if work-related. Employers have legal duty to protect workers from noise >85 dB(A) (Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005).

title: Audiogram interpretation – Key patterns
content: Audiogram interpretation: normal hearing threshold <25 dB HL. Conductive hearing loss: air conduction (AC) thresholds elevated; bone conduction (BC) normal; air-bone gap present. Sensorineural hearing loss: both AC and BC thresholds elevated; no air-bone gap; BC = AC. Mixed hearing loss: both AC and BC elevated; air-bone gap present. Key patterns: presbycusis — bilateral high-frequency SNHL (sloping); noise-induced — bilateral notch at 4 kHz; otosclerosis — conductive HL with Carhart notch at 2 kHz; Ménière's disease — low-frequency SNHL (fluctuating); acoustic neuroma — unilateral high-frequency SNHL.

title: Stridor – Differential diagnosis by age
content: Differential diagnosis of stridor: neonates/infants — laryngomalacia (most common; inspiratory; worse supine/feeding; resolves by 18–24 months), subglottic stenosis (congenital or post-intubation), vocal cord paralysis, vascular ring; children — croup (viral; barking cough; worse at night; 6 months–3 years), epiglottitis (bacterial; rapid onset; drooling; toxic; do NOT examine), inhaled foreign body (sudden onset; unilateral wheeze; asymmetric breath sounds), bacterial tracheitis (Staphylococcus aureus; toxic; purulent secretions); adults — laryngeal carcinoma, thyroid goitre, anaphylaxis, angioedema.

title: Neck lump – Diagnostic approach
content: Diagnostic approach to neck lump: history — duration, rate of growth, associated symptoms (fever, weight loss, dysphagia, hoarseness, otalgia), risk factors (smoking, alcohol, age >40). Examination — site (anterior/posterior triangle, midline/lateral), consistency (soft, firm, hard), mobility, tenderness, transillumination, pulsatility, skin changes. Investigations: FBC, CRP, ESR, LFTs, TFTs, monospot; ultrasound (first-line imaging); FNAC or core biopsy; CT/MRI neck; PET-CT for unknown primary; panendoscopy (direct laryngoscopy, oesophagoscopy, bronchoscopy). 2-week wait referral: any unexplained neck lump in adult; lump in parotid/submandibular gland.

title: Thyroglossal cyst – Management
content: Management of thyroglossal cyst: Sistrunk procedure (surgical excision of cyst, tract, and central portion of hyoid bone — reduces recurrence rate from 50% to <5%). Complications if untreated: infection (thyroglossal abscess), malignant transformation (rare — papillary thyroid carcinoma most common). Pre-operative thyroid imaging recommended to confirm normal thyroid tissue present (as thyroglossal cyst may represent only functional thyroid tissue in some patients).

title: Laryngeal carcinoma – Clinical features and management
content: Laryngeal carcinoma: most common type is squamous cell carcinoma. Risk factors: smoking (most important), alcohol, HPV infection, asbestos exposure. Types: glottic (most common — vocal cord; presents early with hoarseness; good prognosis); supraglottic (presents late — dysphagia, neck lump, referred otalgia; worse prognosis); subglottic (rare; presents with airway obstruction). Features: persistent hoarseness (>3 weeks — urgent 2WW referral for age ≥45 years), dysphagia, stridor, neck lump, weight loss. Investigations: laryngoscopy + biopsy; CT/MRI neck and chest. Management: early disease — radiotherapy or endoscopic laser surgery; advanced disease — total laryngectomy ± radiotherapy/chemotherapy.

title: Vocal cord nodules and polyps – Clinical features and management
content: Vocal cord nodules (singer's nodules): bilateral, symmetrical benign lesions at junction of anterior and middle thirds of vocal cords. Caused by vocal overuse/misuse. Features: hoarseness, voice fatigue, reduced vocal range. Management: voice rest, speech therapy (first-line); surgical excision if conservative treatment fails. Vocal cord polyps: usually unilateral; associated with smoking, vocal overuse, hypothyroidism, GORD. Features: hoarseness. Management: treat underlying cause; surgical excision (microlaryngoscopy).

title: Dysphagia – Differential diagnosis and red flags
content: Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) differential diagnosis: oropharyngeal (neuromuscular — stroke, motor neurone disease, myasthenia gravis, Parkinson's; structural — tonsillitis, peritonsillar abscess, epiglottitis, pharyngeal pouch, head and neck cancer); oesophageal (mechanical — oesophageal carcinoma, benign stricture, Schatzki ring, extrinsic compression; motility — achalasia, diffuse oesophageal spasm, systemic sclerosis). Red flags requiring urgent investigation: progressive dysphagia, weight loss, haematemesis, anaemia, age >55 years with new dysphagia. 2-week wait referral for suspected upper GI cancer.

title: Anosmia – Causes and management
content: Anosmia (loss of smell) causes: nasal/sinonasal (most common — rhinitis, rhinosinusitis, nasal polyps, nasal obstruction); post-viral (COVID-19 most common cause of sudden anosmia; also post-influenza, post-URTI); head trauma (cribriform plate fracture — shearing of olfactory nerve fibres); neurological (Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, multiple sclerosis); congenital (Kallmann syndrome — anosmia + hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism); toxic (smoking, cocaine, medications). Management: treat underlying cause; olfactory training (smell training with 4 distinct odours twice daily for 3+ months — evidence for post-viral anosmia); intranasal corticosteroids (if inflammatory cause); refer to ENT or neurology if persistent.

title: Auricular haematoma – Definition and management
content: Auricular haematoma (cauliflower ear): haematoma between auricular cartilage and perichondrium following blunt trauma to the ear. Common in contact sports (boxing, rugby, wrestling). Features: painful, fluctuant swelling of the auricle; loss of normal auricular contours. Management: urgent drainage (needle aspiration or incision and drainage); compression dressing to prevent reaccumulation; antibiotics to prevent perichondritis. If untreated: fibrosis and calcification → permanent deformity ('cauliflower ear'). Perichondritis: infection of auricular cartilage — most commonly Pseudomonas aeruginosa; treat with ciprofloxacin.

title: Acute sinusitis – Definition and clinical features
content: Acute sinusitis is inflammation of the paranasal sinuses lasting <12 weeks. Most commonly viral (rhinovirus, influenza). Features: facial pain/pressure (worse on bending forward); nasal congestion/obstruction; purulent nasal discharge; reduced sense of smell; headache; post-nasal drip; fever. Maxillary sinus most commonly affected (cheek pain, dental pain). Frontal sinus (forehead pain). Ethmoid sinus (pain between eyes). Sphenoid sinus (vertex/occipital headache). Bacterial sinusitis suggested by: symptoms >10 days, severe symptoms, double-sickening pattern.

title: Cough – ENT causes
content: ENT causes of chronic cough: post-nasal drip (most common ENT cause — rhinitis, rhinosinusitis, nasal polyps; tickling sensation in throat; worse at night; mucus visible in posterior pharynx); laryngopharyngeal reflux (acid irritation of larynx/pharynx; associated hoarseness, globus); vocal cord dysfunction (paradoxical vocal cord motion — inspiratory stridor, throat tightness); laryngeal hypersensitivity; chronic laryngitis; upper airway cough syndrome. Management: treat underlying cause; intranasal corticosteroids and antihistamines for post-nasal drip; PPI trial for LPR.

title: Dizziness – Approach and classification
content: Dizziness is a broad term encompassing: vertigo (illusion of movement — rotatory, most commonly peripheral vestibular cause); presyncope (feeling of impending faint — cardiovascular cause); disequilibrium (unsteadiness without head sensation — cerebellar, proprioceptive, or multisensory); non-specific dizziness (anxiety, hyperventilation, medication side effects). Peripheral vs central vertigo: peripheral (BPPV, vestibular neuronitis, labyrinthitis, Ménière's — sudden onset, severe, fatigable nystagmus, no neurological signs); central (posterior circulation stroke, cerebellar pathology — gradual onset, less severe, non-fatigable nystagmus, neurological signs present).

title: HiNTs examination – Distinguishing peripheral from central vertigo
content: HiNTs (Head Impulse, Nystagmus, Test of Skew) examination: used to distinguish peripheral from central cause of acute vestibular syndrome. Head Impulse test: positive (catch-up saccade) = peripheral; negative (normal VOR) = central (concerning for posterior circulation stroke). Nystagmus: unidirectional horizontal = peripheral; direction-changing or vertical = central. Test of Skew: absent = peripheral; present (vertical misalignment) = central. HiNTs more sensitive than MRI in first 24–48 hours for posterior circulation stroke.

title: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia – ENT features
content: Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT, Osler-Weber-Rendu syndrome): autosomal dominant condition causing abnormal blood vessel formation. ENT features: recurrent epistaxis (most common presenting feature — 90% of patients; begins in childhood; often severe and recurrent); telangiectasias on lips, tongue, nasal mucosa, face, fingers. Systemic features: pulmonary AVMs (haemoptysis, dyspnoea, paradoxical emboli), hepatic AVMs, cerebral AVMs. Management of epistaxis in HHT: humidification, lubricants, cauterisation, laser treatment, bevacizumab (anti-VEGF), septodermoplasty.

title: Paediatric ENT – Common presentations and referral criteria
content: Common paediatric ENT presentations: glue ear (OME) — most common cause of conductive hearing loss in children; croup — viral, barking cough, inspiratory stridor, 6 months–3 years; epiglottitis — bacterial, rapid onset, drooling, toxic; laryngomalacia — most common cause of stridor in neonates; tonsillitis — recurrent, NICE criteria for tonsillectomy; adenoid hypertrophy — nasal obstruction, snoring, OME, recurrent otitis media; inhaled foreign body — sudden onset choking. Referral criteria: hearing loss in child — urgent audiology; stridor in neonate — urgent ENT; suspected epiglottitis — emergency ENT and anaesthetics.

title: Tracheostomy – Indications and complications
content: Tracheostomy indications: upper airway obstruction (tumour, trauma, bilateral vocal cord paralysis, angioedema); prolonged mechanical ventilation (ICU); airway protection (impaired swallowing/cough reflex); pulmonary toilet (secretion management). Types: surgical (standard) vs percutaneous dilatational (bedside, ICU). Complications: immediate — haemorrhage, false passage, pneumothorax, subcutaneous emphysema; early — tube displacement, obstruction, infection, surgical emphysema; late — tracheal stenosis (most common late complication), tracheomalacia, tracheo-oesophageal fistula, tracheo-innominate fistula (life-threatening haemorrhage), decannulation failure.

title: Cochlear implants – Indications and overview
content: Cochlear implants: electronic devices that bypass damaged hair cells and directly stimulate the auditory nerve. Indications (NICE TA166): bilateral severe-profound SNHL (>90 dB HL) in adults who do not benefit adequately from hearing aids; children with bilateral severe-profound SNHL. Components: external (microphone, speech processor, transmitter coil) and internal (receiver-stimulator, electrode array in cochlea). Outcomes: significant improvement in speech understanding; best outcomes with early implantation in children (before age 2 if possible) and short duration of deafness in adults. Contraindications: cochlear ossification, absent auditory nerve.

title: Acoustic neuroma – Epidemiology and investigations
content: Acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) epidemiology: incidence 1–2 per 100,000 per year; accounts for 8% of all intracranial tumours; peak incidence 40–60 years; equal sex distribution. Unilateral in 95% (bilateral = neurofibromatosis type 2). Investigations: pure tone audiogram (asymmetric high-frequency SNHL); auditory brainstem response (ABR — prolonged wave I-V interpeak latency); MRI with gadolinium (gold standard — shows intracanalicular or CPA mass). Management options: observation (small tumours, elderly); stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife); surgical excision (translabyrinthine, retrosigmoid, or middle fossa approach).

title: ENT emergencies – Summary
content: ENT emergencies requiring immediate action: epiglottitis (do NOT examine throat; call anaesthetist and ENT; secure airway); Ludwig's angina (airway management priority; IV antibiotics); post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage (return to theatre if primary; admission and antibiotics if secondary); epistaxis with haemodynamic compromise (resuscitation; posterior packing; surgical ligation); malignant otitis externa with intracranial complications (IV antipseudomonal antibiotics; neurosurgical input); nasal septal haematoma (urgent drainage within 24 hours to prevent cartilage necrosis); auricular haematoma (urgent drainage to prevent cauliflower ear); sudden SNHL (urgent ENT; high-dose steroids within 2 weeks of onset).
